entities.name: John II of Castile
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John II of Castile (1406–1454) reigned as King of Castile and León for an unprecedented 48 years, one of the longest in Castilian history, yet his rule was largely characterized by a continuous struggle for royal authority against a powerful and often rebellious nobility. Born in Toro on March 6, 1405, he inherited the throne as an infant at just 22 months old upon the death of his father, Henry III, plunging the kingdom into a turbulent regency dominated by his mother, Catherine of Lancaster, and his uncle, Ferdinand I of Aragon. His reign, spanning the mid-15th century, marked a critical period in the evolution of the Castilian monarchy, where royal power was severely tested and often overshadowed by the ambitions of magnates like the House of Mendoza and the House of Pacheco, fundamentally shaping the political landscape of the Iberian Peninsula.

The core of John II’s reign was defined by his profound reliance on his favorite and Constable of Castile, Álvaro de Luna, whose influence over the king and administration was immense, effectively governing Castile for much of the period. This concentration of power in a royal favorite, rather than directly by the monarch, fueled intense resentment among the grandees, leading to a series of civil conflicts and conspiracies. The most significant of these was the First Battle of Olmedo in 1445, where royalist forces, predominantly led by Luna, decisively defeated a coalition of Castilian and Aragonese nobles, momentarily reaffirming royal authority but at the cost of deepening the internecine strife within the kingdom.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: John II's exceptionally long reign profoundly weakened the Castilian monarchy and empowered a fractious nobility, directly setting the stage for the later centralizing efforts of the Catholic Monarchs. His era exemplifies the challenges of royal authority in late medieval Iberia, impacting subsequent political developments for decades.
